note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Question b, fact: The why says 'Only parliament can make or change a law'. Point 3 of this chapter teaches that courts can change common law directly, so this overstates the claim. It should say only parliament can pass a bill or make statute law.
- Card, fact: 'It cannot pass or change a law itself, because only parliament can do that' suggests only parliament can change any law. Courts can change common law (point 3), so this should refer to statute law or passing bills.

rejected.title: Parliamentary committees
card: A parliamentary committee is a small group of members of parliament. It looks into a particular issue and reports back to parliament.
Members come from different parties, so a committee can look at an issue with views from across parliament. It can take written submissions, hold public hearings and call witnesses.
After its inquiry, the committee writes a report with findings and recommendations for law reform. Parliament and the government can then decide whether to act on them.
A committee can only recommend. It cannot pass or change a law itself, because only parliament can do that.
rejected.remember: A committee investigates and recommends. Parliament decides whether the law changes.

a.q: What is the main role of a parliamentary committee in law reform?
opts: To investigate an issue and recommend changes to parliament
To pass a bill into law once its inquiry has finished
To decide cases that raise a problem in the law
To make sure the government acts on every recommendation
a.why: A committee inquires into an issue and reports with recommendations. It cannot pass laws, because only parliament can do that, so the option about passing a bill is wrong.
a.clue: Think about what a committee can do with its findings.

b.q: A Victorian parliamentary committee inquires into e-scooter safety and recommends new rules for riders. Who decides whether those rules become law?
opts: Parliament, by voting on a bill
The committee, by approving its report
The courts, by applying the report
Voters, by holding a referendum
b.why: Only parliament can make or change a law, so the rules become law only if parliament passes a bill. The committee is tempting because it wrote the recommendations, but it can only recommend. It has no power to make them law.
b.clue: Who has the power to make a law?

b.q: A Victorian parliamentary committee inquires into e-scooter safety and recommends new rules for riders. What happens next?
opts: Parliament may consider the report and decide whether to act
The recommended rules become law once the report is tabled
The committee drafts the rules and brings them into force
The courts must apply the recommended rules to riders
b.why: The committee has only made recommendations in its report. Parliament and the government decide whether to act, so the rules do not become law just because the report is tabled.
b.clue: Who has the power to make a law?

a.best: To investigate an issue and recommend changes to parliament

b.best: Parliament may consider the report and decide whether to act

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a hedge ('may'). The other three are absolute claims ('become law', 'must apply', 'brings them into force'), so a test-wise student could pick it without knowing the idea.
